title: Assembly
subtitle: x86-64 assembly on Linux, from a first system call to reading what compilers write, with a look at ARM64 and RISC-V.
description: An assembly language is a readable spelling of a processor's machine code: one line, one instruction, with names instead of numbers. There is no single assembly language. Every processor family has its own, and this course teaches the one inside most laptops, desktops and servers: **x86-64**, written for **Linux** with the **GNU assembler** in Intel syntax, with no C library underneath. You will talk to the operating system directly through system calls, build every number you print digit by digit, and learn the calling convention that lets assembly and C call each other. The last lessons compare x86-64 with **ARM64** and **RISC-V** and end with a complete program.

Few people write whole programs in assembly today. Many professionals read it every week: compiler and runtime engineers, people tuning hot loops, security researchers reversing malware or writing exploits for authorised tests, embedded engineers bringing up a new board, and anyone who has stared at a crash in a debugger. This course assumes the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience: you know what a variable, a loop and a function are. Knowing a little C helps in the later lessons but is not required.

To run the programs you need an x86-64 Linux system with GNU Binutils (the `binutils` package on Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora). On Windows, WSL 2 gives you one; on a Mac, use a Linux virtual machine or an x86-64 Linux container. There is no official online playground for assembly, but [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org/) shows the assembly that compilers produce for any C function you type, and it is used throughout the later lessons.

levels.title: Talking to the processor
levels.summary: What assembly is and why it is still worth learning, then registers, arithmetic, memory, addressing, flags and jumps: enough to compute anything and print the answer.

levels.title: Functions, the kernel and the compiler
levels.summary: The stack and the System V calling convention, system calls as the door into the kernel, and how assembly and C call each other and how to read what a compiler writes.

levels.title: Other machines and a complete program
levels.summary: How ARM64 and RISC-V differ from x86-64 and why, then a complete text-statistics tool in idiomatic x86-64 with notes on debugging, performance and where to go next.

references.title: Using as: the GNU Assembler manual
references.note: The official manual for the assembler used in this course, including its directives and the x86 Intel-syntax notes.

references.title: Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manuals
references.author: Intel
references.note: The definitive description of every x86-64 instruction. Volume 1 explains the architecture; Volume 2 is the instruction reference.

references.title: System V Application Binary Interface, AMD64 Architecture Processor Supplement
references.note: The calling convention and binary interface used by Linux on x86-64.

references.title: syscall(2) and syscalls(2), Linux manual pages
references.note: How each architecture passes system-call numbers and arguments, and the list of Linux system calls.

references.title: Compiler Explorer
references.note: Type C, C++, Rust or many other languages and see the assembly that real compilers produce, side by side.
